title: Editorial: The Stormers get it. The Proteas less so. What can wine learn?
summary:
I’ve spent the past three Saturdays at DHL Stadium watching the Stormers, and I can assure you they’re doing something right. The post Editorial: The Stormers get it. The Proteas less so. What can wine learn? appeared first on winemag.
content:
I’ve spent the past three Saturdays at DHL Stadium watching the Stormers, and I can assure you they’re doing something right. The Proteas, by contrast, have some soul-searching to do when it comes to attracting crowds to Test cricket.

For the South African wine industry, which is trying to arrest declining consumption and build a meaningful export business, the contrast is instructive. The Stormers show how supporting a team can become a compelling social experience that builds lasting loyalty; the empty stands at Kingsmead suggest that tradition and national pride are not enough to guarantee an audience. Wine faces a similar challenge: making itself relevant to how people want to live today. Producing good wine is no longer enough, if it ever was.

The Stormers averaged 26,153 spectators per game in the 2025/26 United Rugby Championship season, the highest regular-season average in the competition for the third time in five seasons. The first Test between South Africa and Australia at Kingsmead in October, by contrast, attracted fewer than 20,000 spectators over five days. The comparison is imperfect: a five-day Test is a different proposition from a rugby fixture, and Kingsmead attendance was affected by timing, the cost of travel and refreshments, and disruption in Durban. Nevertheless, the contrast is striking.

It is also worth remembering how close professional rugby in the Western Cape came to financial ruin. Western Province Rugby accumulated substantial debt, made poor financial decisions and failed to secure a sustainable way forward. By 2021, SA Rugby had placed the union under administration. Western Province and the Stormers have long been woven into Cape Town’s identity, with generations of supporters invested in their fortunes. It would have been absurd if maladministration had been allowed to destroy a franchise so deeply embedded in the life of the city. The professional rugby operation was eventually taken over by a consortium of investors that included the family of Capitec founder Michiel le Roux. The deal brought in new capital and a different ownership structure, with the aim of putting the Stormers on a more sustainable footing.

New owners do not automatically make better leaders, but the crisis demanded accountability and a willingness to change. The Stormers’ emerging success rests not just on what happens on the field, but on an organisation capable of making decisions and delivering an experience supporters want to return to. Financial recovery and sporting achievement are different things, but both require effective management.

Wine’s leadership problem

The wine industry has its own existential concerns, yet its leadership is considerably more diffuse. Producers, industry bodies, trade and government all have a stake in the sector’s future, but no single organisation has an uncontested mandate to set priorities and be held accountable for reversing declining domestic consumption or building a coherent export programme. The result is too often research, strategy documents and familiar calls for collaboration, with less clarity about who will act.

The current dispute over SAWIS’s certification contract illustrates the problem. The Wine Certification Authority’s decision to terminate its service agreement with SAWIS has raised concerns about the continuity and cost of essential certification and inspection services. South Africa Wine says it was not adequately consulted and has sought legal advice while raising its concerns with the Minister of Agriculture. The full implications remain unclear, but the dispute has exposed tensions between organisations whose cooperation is essential to the industry’s functioning. If the industry struggles to coordinate an essential service, how can it mount a coherent response to the much larger challenges facing its domestic and export markets?

The urgency is clear. South African wine consumption fell by 7.7% in 2025, according to the International Organisation of Vine and Wine. Cost-of-living pressures, changing attitudes to alcohol and competition from other drinks all play a part. So does the declining relevance of wine to people who no longer regard it as an automatic part of social life. These trends cannot simply be marketed away, but neither can the industry afford to treat them as inevitable.

The Stormers understand that a match is an occasion, not merely a contest. The rugby matters, but so do the atmosphere, the shared allegiance and the experience of being there. The club has cultivated a regional identity and given supporters reasons to feel involved beyond the 80 minutes. The product is not just rugby; it is interpersonal engagement.

Wine has quality, history, regional identity and extraordinary diversity. Yet much of the industry’s communication remains directed at people who already understand and care about it. We talk to one another about terroir, heritage, sustainability and premiumisation, then wonder why the wider public seems indifferent. The industry is more comfortable explaining why wine deserves respect than asking why someone who knows little about it should choose a bottle tonight.

The obvious remedies, making wine more accessible, selling the occasion and building loyalty, have been discussed for years. Why, then, has so little changed? Repeating the advice is less useful than examining the obstacles to putting it into practice.

Why the industry struggles to change

One obstacle is structural. The industry comprises hundreds of producers, many small businesses fighting for survival. Each has an incentive to promote its own wines, but less incentive to invest in growing the category as a whole when competitors will benefit too. This is the collective-action problem: the benefits are shared, while the costs fall on those who contribute.

A second obstacle is that the industry has no single set of priorities. Exporters and domestic producers, large companies and small cellars, premium brands and value-focused businesses may all want South African wine to prosper, but they will not necessarily agree on how to achieve it or who should pay. Without an agreed direction, a mandate to lead and accountability for results, collaboration can become an end in itself rather than a means of getting things done.

There is also a cultural obstacle. Wine can be overly attached to its own importance. Expertise, heritage and technical accomplishment are genuine strengths, but they can celebrated for the sake of it. Making wine more relevant requires more than simplified messaging. It means understanding the occasions, budgets and preferences of people outside the industry’s traditional audience, and being prepared to change the offer accordingly.

The Stormers’ experience suggests that recovery starts with confronting an organisation’s problems, not merely promoting its virtues. Their financial crisis required new capital, ownership and a more sustainable operating model. Building supporter loyalty then had a foundation on which to work. Wine, by contrast, too often treats declining consumption as a communications problem when it is also a problem of incentives, governance and execution.

The wine industry does not suffer from a shortage of ideas. It suffers from a shortage of leadership willing to make choices, commit resources and accept responsibility when those choices fail. The uncomfortable question is not what wine should do next. It is why, having known for so long what needs doing, it has been so reluctant to do it.

title: Jean Engelbrecht appointed Stellenbosch Wine Routes chair
summary:
Jean Engelbrecht of Rust en Vrede has been appointed chair of Stellenbosch Wine Routes, succeeding Mike Ratcliffe, who steps down after nine years. The change was announced at the organisation’s AGM on 21 October. Louw Strydom of Kanonkop replaces Chris Boustred of Remhoogte, while Frans Smit of Spier and Bruwer Raats of Raats Family Wines […]

The post Jean Engelbrecht appointed Stellenbosch Wine Routes chair appeared first on winemag.
content:
Mike Ratcliffe and Jean Engelbrecht.

Jean Engelbrecht of Rust en Vrede has been appointed chair of Stellenbosch Wine Routes, succeeding Mike Ratcliffe, who steps down after nine years. The change was announced at the organisation’s AGM on 21 October.

Louw Strydom of Kanonkop replaces Chris Boustred of Remhoogte, while Frans Smit of Spier and Bruwer Raats of Raats Family Wines join the board. Ilse Ruthford of Compagniesdrift departs.

Established in 1971, Stellenbosch Wine Routes represents wine producers across five sub-routes: Bottelary Hills, Greater Simonsberg, Helderberg, Stellenbosch Valley and Stellenbosch Berg.

The board for 2027 comprises:

  • Jean Engelbrecht (Rust en Vrede, chair)

  • Amanda de Klerk (vice-chair)

  • Danie Steytler (Kaapzicht)

  • David van Velden (Overgaauw)

  • Carina Gous (Kleine Zalze)

  • Schalk-Willem Joubert (Taaibosch)

  • Louw Strydom (Kanonkop)

  • Ntsiki Biyela (Aslina Wines)

  • Bruwer Raats (Raats Family Wines)

  • Nic van Aarde (Oldenburg Wines)

  • Frans Smit (Spier)

title: Tim James: Travels and wine – a few irritations, some great bottles
summary:
Something was needed, I thought, to jolt me from my rut. So I resolved on a rare foreign break, despite all the awfulness and anxiety (as it seemed from the rut perspective) of arrangements and airports. Not a calculatedly wine trip but, for a wine person, consciousness of wine inevitably intrudes. It did so from […]

The post Tim James: Travels and wine – a few irritations, some great bottles appeared first on winemag.
content:
Something was needed, I thought, to jolt me from my rut. So I resolved on a rare foreign break, despite all the awfulness and anxiety (as it seemed from the rut perspective) of arrangements and airports.

Not a calculatedly wine trip but, for a wine person, consciousness of wine inevitably intrudes. It did so from the start, in the usual way, with anger and irritation at seeing the cost of wine in the “Big Five Duty Free” shop at Cape Town airport. Duty- free perhaps, but they more than make up for it by piling on the profit they extract from home-bound tourists, who pay vastly more than they would do in a bottle-store in town. As examples, take Jordan Sophia selling there for R755 compared with the usual R600-odd; or Donkiesbaai Steen for R475 instead of around R350. This appallingly greedy cynicism is actually a real scandal, I think, one that the tourism industry should look into and protest at. (Shareholders include German travel retailer Gebr. Heinemann; luxury distributor and retailer CAVI Brands; a women-owned investment consortium including Zithezava and Rumbi Investments; and Maponya Investment Holdings.)

The grumpy news continued on the KLM flight to Amsterdam, with narrower seats than I remembered or even thought possible. The only positive thing to say about the little dinky plastic bottle of red wine was that it was a good match for the awful food. If it hadn’t caused such a bother when I knocked over the “glass” and splashed it over myself – and inevitably a little over my neighbour – I could cheerfully have just said good riddance. I certainly didn’t ask for more.

Wine, airports and the cost of travel

On the other hand, duty-free wine shelves in European airports seem to be up a little from their nadir – though nowhere like they were when, for example, Berry Bros had a branch at Heathrow (I remember buying well-priced bottles of DRC Grands Echezeaux and Hugel Clos Ste Hune there a few decades back). I should have bought a bottle or two at Schipol when waiting for my London connection: I could have done better, in terms of price and with a few years on the bottle, than at Waitrose in Bloomsbury.

Not that I was eating or drinking much in my six nights in a small flat – my bottle of Rioja Beronia Reserva lasted me for a few meals. More delicious and interesting, I thought, was the bottle of Ollieux Romanis Soufle de Lune 2022 Corbières I shared with a London-based South African friend who took me to a cheerfully packed little French bistro in Soho for dinner (delicious food too).

I was very generously treated on this trip, in fact. Next day I was extravagantly indulged by a good friend who has a taste (and pocket) for rather grand establishment places. After breakfast at Simpsons on the Strand, and then some good walking and a morning at the Wallace Collection, my favourite public gallery in London, we lunched, lightly and smartly, at The Wolseley “café-restaurant” in Mayfair (in what had been the 1920s showroom of Wolseley Motors) – I with a salade niçoise. There I had, in fact, my sole wine for the day – a glass of good champagne, which was exactly the right thing after the morning’s exertions. I’m not a devoted sparkling-wine person, but this was perfectly suited. No wine in the evening, as we went to a Chinese restaurant for dinner and drank Chinese beer (with a large neighbouring table of Chinese people making a fearsome amount of noise as they downed rice-wine spirits of alarming strength – which was confirmed when we checked the discarded bottles later, after they’d moved on).

A 60-year-old GS Cabernet makes the journey worthwhile

The wine highlight of my visit came the next day when I spent a wonderful evening with my friend Neil Beckett, illustrious editor of the World of Fine Wine. We hadn’t seen each other for a decade or more, but the time fell away, helped by a copious flow of serious wine and the excellent, elegant meal he prepared after a day’s work. Spanish ham with JJ Prüm Wehlener Sonnenuhr Kabinett – still quite fruitily youthful and delicious; then scallops with a remarkable Chablis, Raveneau Montée de Tonnerre 1996. To my taste it showed just a touch too developed on the nose, but the fine, richly acidic palate was splendid.

Then, with grouse (a rare treat for a colonial!), the wine that I’d brought over, my last bottle of GS Cabernet 1966 (a rare treat for the metropolitan!). It had a very promising, high-shoulder, ullage and the cork came out fine with a little encouragement, and the wine was as good as I’d hoped. Nearly two decades ago, I’d drunk both vintages of GS (66 and 68) at dinner with Neil and fellow-Brit Stephen Spurrier, who’d both come out to judge on the Trophy Wine Show, with Louise Hofmeyr of Welgemeend, who’d supplied the wines from her cellar – it was still quite early days in GS’s fame and cultism. Both wines were spectacular then and so was the 1966 in London last week, 60 years after its harvest – darkly rich and full-flavoured, amazingly fresh and lively, with fully resolved tannins but no sign of tiring. Just a little was left in the bottle when we returned to the whites to accompany some splendid English cheeses. Great wines, company and food. Sometimes it’s foolish to save a wine for a special occasion, and then sometimes it’s fully worth it. My 2am Uber took me back to Bloomsbury exhilarated and happy.

 

And so, via Eurostar, to Paris – “on fire”, the papers said, but not in Montmartre, where I spent my mere two days. And there I realised that, because I’d thought only of being in a flat in London, I had neglected to bring my usual basic equipment for dealing with hotel room eating: sharp knife, fork, spoon, corkscrew and a decent wineglass. But good food and wine was easily available, of course – I was pleased to see, despite declines in French wine consumption, that all the many little corner shops had a few shelves of wine. And the smallish supermarket around the corner had, in fact, a pretty good selection (all French, of course), from which I chose a very pleasing 2021 St-Julien, the second label of Ch Lagrange. I bought a corkscrew to open it, but it had to suffer the indignity of being drunk from the green plastic tumbler from my bathroom.

More Bordeaux for me from the duty-free at Charles De Gaulle airport – a good shop, unlike the exploitative set-up in Cape Town. Wider seats and better food and wine (an acceptable French merlot) on Air France – and, bless them, they even offered a tiny bottle of cognac after the meal. Vive la France! Back home to the dogs and to settle down in my comfortable rut once more. First dinner back, to welcome myself I opened a bottle of Van Loggerenberg Graft 2017– the maiden vintage, which included cinsault along with the syrah. No problem there; none at all.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

content:
Something was needed, I thought, to jolt me from my rut. So I resolved on a rare foreign break, despite all the awfulness and anxiety (as it seemed from the rut perspective) of arrangements and airports.

I was very generously treated on this trip, in fact. Next day I was extravagantly indulged by a good friend who has a taste (and pocket) for rather grand establishment places. After breakfast at Simpsons on the Strand, and then some good walking and a morning at the Wallace Collection, my favourite public gallery in London, we lunched, lightly and smartly, at The Wolseley “café-restaurant” in Mayfair (in what had been the 1920s showroom of Wolseley Motors) – I with a salade niçoise. There I had, in fact, my sole wine for the day – a glass of good champagne, which was exactly the right thing after the morning’s exertions. I’m not a devoted sparkling-wine person, but this was perfectly suited. No wine in the evening, as we went to a Chinese restaurant for dinner and drank Chinese beer (with a large neighbouring table of Chinese people making a fearsome amount of noise as they downed rice-wine spirits of alarming strength – which was confirmed when we checked the discarded bottles later, after they’d moved on).

A 60-year-old GS Cabernet makes the journey worthwhile

The wine highlight of my visit came the next day when I spent a wonderful evening with my friend Neil Beckett, illustrious editor of the World of Fine Wine. We hadn’t seen each other for a decade or more, but the time fell away, helped by a copious flow of serious wine and the excellent, elegant meal he prepared after a day’s work. Spanish ham with JJ Prüm Wehlener Sonnenuhr Kabinett – still quite fruitily youthful and delicious; then scallops with a remarkable Chablis, Raveneau Montée de Tonnerre 1996. To my taste it showed just a touch too developed on the nose, but the fine, richly acidic palate was splendid.

Then, with grouse (a rare treat for a colonial!), the wine that I’d brought over, my last bottle of GS Cabernet 1966 (a rare treat for the metropolitan!). It had a very promising, high-shoulder, ullage and the cork came out fine with a little encouragement, and the wine was as good as I’d hoped. Nearly two decades ago, I’d drunk both vintages of GS (66 and 68) at dinner with Neil and fellow-Brit Stephen Spurrier, who’d both come out to judge on the Trophy Wine Show, with Louise Hofmeyr of Welgemeend, who’d supplied the wines from her cellar – it was still quite early days in GS’s fame and cultism. Both wines were spectacular then and so was the 1966 in London last week, 60 years after its harvest – darkly rich and full-flavoured, amazingly fresh and lively, with fully resolved tannins but no sign of tiring. Just a little was left in the bottle when we returned to the whites to accompany some splendid English cheeses. Great wines, company and food. Sometimes it’s foolish to save a wine for a special occasion, and then sometimes it’s fully worth it. My 2am Uber took me back to Bloomsbury exhilarated and happy.

 

And so, via Eurostar, to Paris – “on fire”, the papers said, but not in Montmartre, where I spent my mere two days. And there I realised that, because I’d thought only of being in a flat in London, I had neglected to bring my usual basic equipment for dealing with hotel room eating: sharp knife, fork, spoon, corkscrew and a decent wineglass. But good food and wine was easily available, of course – I was pleased to see, despite declines in French wine consumption, that all the many little corner shops had a few shelves of wine. And the smallish supermarket around the corner had, in fact, a pretty good selection (all French, of course), from which I chose a very pleasing 2021 St-Julien, the second label of Ch Lagrange. I bought a corkscrew to open it, but it had to suffer the indignity of being drunk from the green plastic tumbler from my bathroom.

More Bordeaux for me from the duty-free at Charles De Gaulle airport – a good shop, unlike the exploitative set-up in Cape Town. Wider seats and better food and wine (an acceptable French merlot) on Air France – and, bless them, they even offered a tiny bottle of cognac after the meal. Vive la France! Back home to the dogs and to settle down in my comfortable rut once more. First dinner back, to welcome myself I opened a bottle of Van Loggerenberg Graft 2017– the maiden vintage, which included cinsault along with the syrah. No problem there; none at all.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.
